tagline: Around the harbor, the working city keeps its tools.
intro: From Locust Point toward Fells Point, the drive rounds a harbor shaped by industry and immigration. Fort McHenry holds the end of the Locust Point peninsula, where it turned back British warships in September 1814. The Domino sugar factory nearby shows the harbor still works for a living.

Across the water, the Fells Point yards built fast topsail schooners known as Baltimore clippers, more than 150 of them between 1810 and 1815. Many sailed as privateers against British shipping, which helped bring the British to Baltimore in 1814.

moments.title: Locust Point
moments.text: From 1868 until the piers closed in 1914, 1.2 million European immigrants came ashore here, and the neighborhood earned the name Baltimore's Ellis Island.

moments.title: Baltimore Museum of Industry
moments.text: An old oyster cannery holds recreated workshops and the pharmacy where Noxzema was invented; at its dock lies the 1906 steam tug Baltimore, which can no longer leave.

moments.title: Fells Point
moments.text: Frederick Douglass taught himself to read here as a boy, copying the letters shipyard men marked on boards, and in 1835 he was hired out to caulk ships in the same yards.
